extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry and literary criticism; poets seeking Aristotelian principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic works according to Aristotelian and related critical principles (probability, unity, imitation, representation of the universal, and the end of fine art). Useful for poets, critics, and students applying Poetics-derived standards to drama, epic, and comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of chance and improbable incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance (τὸ συμβεβηκός) and 'improbable possibilities' are banished from poetry; poetry 'prohibits the introduction of any such anomalies of experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce incidents that appear to occur 'by strange chance' or that are merely anomalous experiences. Exception only when the poet's skill can 'impart to it an appearance of design.' Comedy's incidents may be looser but still 'framed on lines of probability' and are not mere accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth: idealised but law-abiding representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'presents permanent and eternal facts' and 'may transcend nature, but he may not contradict her; he must not be disobedient to her habits and principles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet may recreate the actual and pass the bounds of reality, yet must avoid the lawless, the fantastic, and the impossible; poetic truth 'passes the bounds of reality, but it does not wantonly violate the laws which make the real world rational.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and organic wholeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetic creation must exhibit unity and plurality: 'a unity which is unfolded and expanded according to the law of its own nature, an organism which develops from within.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts must be inwardly connected, arranged in a certain order, structurally related, and combined into a system. A whole is not a mere mass of transposable parts. Balance size: if too small the whole is perceived but not the parts; if too large the parts are perceived but not the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure: single complete action with beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot 'must as in a tragedy be dramatically constructed; it must have for its object a single action whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the plot so it resembles a living organism: a single action that produces the appropriate pleasure. Dramatic construction requires that events be ordered to show causal and thematic unity rather than a mere sequence of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal necessity and logical/moral connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's drama postulates an unbroken chain of cause and effect: necessity is 'logical and moral necessity, binding together the successive moments of a life, the parts of an action, into a significant unity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each link in the plot should arise from the contact of human will with outward surroundings; avoid reliance on accident. The law of 'the probable' as well as of 'the necessary' excludes chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the universal through the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'is a more philosophical and a higher thing than history' because it approaches the universal; its aim is 'to represent the universal through the particular' and to give a concrete, sensuous embodiment of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aim to state abstract universals; instead, transfigure particular cases so that universal forms and truths 'steal access through our senses to our minds.' The universal should be manifest through vivid, particularized imagery and organized action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be representative yet particularised
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in poetry must be 'clothed with generic attributes' or 'class characteristics' that are 'so modified and particularised in each person ... that life itself does not excite more distinctly that sense of individuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters traits that are probable from their situation (representative of a class) while still highly individualized. Avoid mere abstraction; the 'individual form' should be uppermost even as it embodies class-relevant universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form dominates matter; proportion and appropriate size
rubrics_metrics.description: Form (essence) governs matter; the quantity of matter and size of parts are determined by the form of the whole. Artistic composition must observe proportion and exclude components that disrupt symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose materials and scale according to the form's needs. Exclude elements that conspicuously surpass or unbalance the composition (analogy: a conductor excluding an overly beautiful solo voice). Size and proportion should serve the unity and beauty of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the monstrous and gratuitous grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Monstrous or 'teratōdes' elements—abortive efforts, strange and monstrous growths, 'failures of the principle of design'—are condemned in tragedy and generally unsuitable to poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce grotesque or monstrous incidents for shock alone; deviations from nature may be occasionally defensible historically, but scientifically and artistically they are not 'natural' and should not be endorsed as proper poetic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of composition: abstraction from particulars to reveal universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle advises setting forth the plot 'in its general idea (ἐκτίθεσθαι καθόλου), abstracting the accidental features of time, place, and persons, and afterwards to fill it in with detail and incident and with proper names.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from a particular story, disentangle the main outline, add or omit elements for artistic purposes, then particularize. The method is not to impose an abstract idea onto particulars, but to generalize the particular by artistic treatment so it embodies the universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of fine art: pleasure / rational enjoyment (πρὸς ἡδονήν)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle draws a sharp distinction between useful arts and fine arts: 'The end of the fine arts is to give pleasure (πρὸς ἡδονήν) or rational enjoyment (πρὸς διαγωγήν).' Fine art's end is not utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different kinds of pleasure (higher and lower). Fine art may incidentally produce useful or moral effects, but its true end is pleasurable/rational enjoyment suited to leisure and the higher kinds of pleasurable activity.
